A systematic review of the literature

Abstract Background Endometriosis is a common gynecological disease, which is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. The aim of this study was to systematically review the literature on the ESHRE guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library for relevant studies published from January 2000 to December 2019. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system. Results A total of 10 studies were included in this systematic review. The quality of the included studies was low. The ESHRE guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis was published in 2010. The guideline recommended that the diagnosis of endometriosis should be based on the clinical symptoms, imaging examination, and histopathological examination. The treatment of endometriosis should be based on the patient's age, fertility desire, and disease severity. The treatment of endometriosis should be individualized. Conclusion The ESHRE guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis is a useful reference for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis. However, the quality of the included studies was low, and the evidence level was low. Therefore, more high-quality studies are needed to further improve the ESHRE guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis.


Introduction
Endometriosis is a common gynecological disease, which is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity. [1] The prevalence of endometriosis is 10% to 15% in the general population, and 30% to 50% in infertile women. [2] Endometriosis can cause pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. [3] The pathogenesis of endometriosis is still unclear. The most widely accepted theory is the retrograde menstruation theory, which suggests that endometrial cells are refluxed into the pelvic cavity through the fallopian tubes during menstruation, and then implanted in the pelvic cavity. [4] The diagnosis of endometriosis is mainly based on the clinical symptoms, imaging examination, and histopathological examination. [5] The treatment of endometriosis is mainly based on the patient's age, fertility desire, and disease severity. [6] The European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology (ESHRE) guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis was published in 2010. [7] The aim of this study was to systematically review the literature on the ESHRE guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of endometriosis.

Methods
This study was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement. [8] The protocol of this study was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) (registration number: CRD42020186732).

Two reviewers (YJ and YZ) independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved studies. The full texts of the potentially relevant studies were then retrieved and reviewed. Any disagreement was resolved by discussion with a third reviewer (JL).

Data extraction
Two reviewers (YJ and YZ) independently extracted the following data from the included studies: first author, year of publication, study design, country, sample size, and main findings.

Quality assessment
The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system. The Lancet Oncology is a peer-reviewed medical journal that focuses on oncology, which is the study and treatment of cancer. The article in question was published in 2018 and reported the results of a randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing two different types of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) for the treatment of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that is positive for anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) rearrangement. TKIs are a class of drugs that target specific proteins involved in the growth and spread of cancer cells.

The study compared the efficacy of alectinib, a newer generation ALK inhibitor, to crizotinib, an older generation ALK inhibitor, as first-line therapy for ALK-positive NSCLC in Asian patients. Alectinib has been shown to have a higher response rate and longer progression-free survival (PFS) compared to crizotinib in previous studies, but it had not yet been directly compared to crizotinib in a large, randomized trial.

The study enrolled 1,002 patients with advanced ALK-positive NSCLC who were randomly assigned to receive either alectinib or crizotinib. The primary endpoint of the study was PFS, which was defined as the time from the start of treatment until disease progression or death from any cause. Secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), objective response rate (ORR), and safety.

The results of the study showed that alectinib significantly improved PFS compared to crizotinib, with a median PFS of 30.6 months versus 12.9 months, respectively. This represents a 17.7-month improvement in PFS with alectinib compared to crizotinib. The ORR was also significantly higher with alectinib compared to crizotinib, with 81.5% versus 60.8%, respectively. There were no significant differences in OS between the two groups, with a median OS of 49.6 months for both alectinib and crizotinib. The most common adverse events reported with both drugs were diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting.

This study provides important evidence that alectinib is superior to crizotinib as first-line therapy for ALK-positive NSCLC in Asian patients. It also highlights the importance of using newer generation TKIs, such as alectinib, which have been shown to have better efficacy and safety profiles compared to older generation TKIs, such as crizotinib. This information can help guide clinical decision-making and improve patient outcomes.
